title: Moderating IEA View Limiting Tanker Outlook

summary:
outlook would pressure
In its recent Oil Market Report (OMR), the International Energy Agency (IEA) kept its forecast for 2012 global oil demand roughly unchanged, while lowering its estimates for 2013 global oil demand growth from those levels previously reported in its medium term outlooks. Given its expectations for growth in non-OPEC supply and OPEC natural gas Liquids (NGLs), the IEA forecast call on OPEC crude in 2013 remains unchanged from 2012. With OPEC maintaining aggressive output levels to promote massive global stock builds in 1h12, any return to normalised inventory management during 2012-13 would suggest a sharp drop in OPEC production in the Arabian Gulf (AG).

children.summary: evolved from credit party, to optimism and now to realism exited recession. Since mid-2011, however, the agency has downgraded its oil demand growth expectations, as the global economy wrestles with structural issues still unresolved from the financial crisis.

children.title: IEA has untethered itself
children.summary: In fact, the IMF's almost triumphalist perspective on the rebounding strength of the recovery led them to argue that global economic growth could grow indefinitely at 4.5%, despite a lengthy deleveraging process and structural issues facing the OECD economies. In turn, this Panglossian view led to IEA forecasts of 1.2 mbpd annual oil demand growth, extending almost indefinitely in its medium-term outlooks.

children.title: Rising Americas crude
children.summary: production pressuring call on OPEC crude A static call on OPEC crude is hardly supportive for the tanker market, particularly with the cartel currently producing more than 1 mbpd above this level. Aggressive OPEC output levels that averaged 31.58 mbpd during 1h12 provided implied global stock builds of 1.3 mbpd and 2.1 mbpd in 1q12 and 2q12, respectively, in response to growing market anxiety over Iranian sanctions.

children.title: OPEC production push
children.summary: prompted massive stock build, mostly in non- OECD locations The implications for AG crude exports and VLCCs could be challenging, given modest yoy gains in OPEC output in Libya and Angola expected for 2013. A 0.80 mbpd decline in OPEC production might imply a 0.95 mbpd cut in AG output, removing at least 2.5% from crude tanker demand, predominantly for VLCCs.

children.title: Static inventories would
children.summary: require large cut in AG exports In the near term, the current malaise in the VLCC market may be reflecting a pause in inventory building, or perhaps something more sustained. The 1.7 mbpd average stock build in 1h12 added 300 million tonnes of additional cargo during the period, mostly in form of exaggerated OPEC production flowing from the AG to Asian locations.
